newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Air Afrique boss sees no privatisation before 2002.
newsitem.headline: Air Afrique boss sees no privatisation before 2002.

text.p: The managing director of troubled multinational airline Air Afrique says it must clear its debts before thinking abour privatisation.

Sir Harry Tirvengadum, quoted in Wednesday's Ivory Coast daily Fraternite Matin, said:"The first part of our short term programme is given over to the priority of priorites, that is to say settling our debt arrears.
"I believe we should head for privatisation as soon as the company finances are cleaned up, the debt is rescheduled and we have returned to financial viability."
"We can't balance the budget this year, but I have given myself an objective from here to the year 2000, it is important to balance our budget," he said.

Tirvengadum said that after dealing with the immediate problems, a medium term plan of three to five years would be put in place to prepare for ultimate privatisation. When asked when privatisation could take place he said "not before five years."

He said he hoped a compromise would be found with a possible saviour of the company, French-speaking Africa air safety agency ASECNA, which demands interest payments on money it has agreed to pay into a new leasing company to take over planes and debt.

Air Afrique has debts of some 200 billion CFA francs ($350 million) and was supposed to have paid off 31 billion CFA francs in arrears by the end of last year. A deadline of March 31 set by creditors has also passed without progress being made.

Much of the debt was contracted to buy planes in the early 1990s, but the company hit serious repayment problems of its dollar-denominated debt after the 50 percent devaluation of the CFA franc in 1994.
The recovery plan has been hampered by the fact that, of the 11 member states, only Ivory Coast and Senegal have paid their one billion CFA francs contribution to the new company.
Tirvengadum was appointed at the start of the year after member states effectively sacked his predecessor Yves-Rolland Billecart.

He said there would be no programme of mass lay-offs from the airline, but said staff numbers would have to be reduced from the current level of 4,588 people for 15 planes -- against 1,650 for a dozen aircraft at Air Mauritius, which he previously ran.
"Compared to international norms our production per employee is too low," he said.

In addition to Ivory Coast and Senegal, the states that own Air Afrique are Benin, Burkina Faso, Central African Republic, Congo, Mali, Mauritania, Niger, Chad and Togo. Air France also has a small stake.
